meta.title: MANUSAT: Onboard Edge AI Health Monitoring for CMG Bearing Fault Detection
meta.authorsHtml: Eleonora Mariotti<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Gianluca Furano<sup>1</sup>, Andrea Zanellini<sup>2</sup>, Riccardo Zanella<sup>2</sup>, Mattia Violi<sup>2</sup>, Kevin Russo<sup>3</sup>, Francesco Aldrigo<sup>3</sup>, Riccardo Rovatti<sup>3</sup>, Mauro Mangia<sup>3</sup>

abstract: Early-stage bearing faults in satellite Control Moment Gyroscopes (CMGs) produce high-frequency vibration signatures that cannot be captured through conventional lowrate telemetry and are impractical to downlink due to bandwidth limitations. This paper presents MANUSAT, an edge-computing health monitoring architecture that detects CMG anomalies directly onboard the spacecraft. The system integrates six-axis vibration sensing with an Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based processing unit performing signal acquisition and machine learning inference at the edge. Anomaly detection relies on convolutional autoencoder models trained exclusively on nominal vibration data, using Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) spectrograms as input. The approach is validated on an experimental testbed featuring a modified CMG with an artificially induced outer-race bearing defect. Both model variants achieve perfect class separation, i.e., Area Under the Curve (AUC) = 1, on severe faults; sensitivity to weaker anomalies is further improved by a moving-average confirmation strategy. Deployment on a Commercial Off-The- Shelf (COTS) PolarFire SoC FPGA yields an inference latency of 70 ms, confirming real-time onboard feasibility.

blocks.html: As satellite constellations grow and missions venture further into deep space, continuous ground supervision becomes a bottleneck due to communication latency and bandwidth constraints [1]. In this context, the reliability of onboard actuators is paramount. Control Moment Gyroscopes (CMGs) [2–4], widely employed in Attitude and Orbit Control System (AOCS) [5] for precise and agile attitude control, are particularly critical: an undetected bearing degradation can escalate to a mission-threatening failure.

Conventional health monitoring relies on the Fault Detection, Isolation, and Recovery (FDIR) system, which compares low-frequency telemetry against static thresholds. While computationally light, this approach is inherently reactive: it detects faults only after performance degradation has occurred and cannot identify subtle early-stage anomalies without manual recalibration by ground operators. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques offer a complementary paradigm by analysing high-frequency sensor data to recognize complex degradation patterns before they become critical. However, shifting to a data-driven approach introduces two key challenges: the need for significant onboard computational resources to process high-bandwidth signals, and the scarcity of in-orbit failure data for model training.

The MANUSAT project [6] addresses these challenges through a modular edge-computing architecture. The system integrates high-frequency accelerometers with an Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based processing unit, combining two complementary acquisition layers: standard low-frequency telemetries (temperatures, gimbal and flywheel speeds) and high-frequency vibration signatures inaccessible to conventional telemetry chains. The FPGA fabric enables reconfiguration of both the signal processing pipeline and the ML inference engine without hardware modifications, while the AI models are designed to be pre-trained on ground and fine-tuned in orbit to adapt to mission-specific conditions.

To validate this approach, a training dataset is collected using a functional test bench to simulate both nominal and faulty operational conditions. This setup allows for the verification of the system’s capability to detect earlystage degradation, a critical step towards validating the technology for future flight missions.
This paper presents the development of ML architectures optimized for automated anomaly detection, together with their validation through the analysis of induced physical fault conditions.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the architecture of the MANUSAT system and the HW/SW design. Section 3 presents the CMG testbed and the test campaign. Section 4 details the anomaly detection models, and Section 5 discusses the experimental results.

The experimental setup consists of three logical blocks that interact over a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus network: the Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) CMG, which is the monitored plant generating the mechanical dynamics and vibration signatures under multiple operating conditions; the MANUSAT Health Monitoring Unit (HMU), an FPGA-based avionics module performing synchronous acquisition, pre-processing, and ML inference entirely at the edge; and a host PC emulating the satellite On Board Computer (OBC), which orchestrates the test campaign by sending telecommands to the CMG drivers and to the HMU. A detailed system-level block diagram is provided in [6]; this section focuses on the key design choices of the HMU.

The HMU is implemented on the Microchip MPFS-DISCO- KIT, based on the PolarFire SoC MPFS095T. This platform was selected for two reasons: the PolarFire SoC family is aligned with the ESA roadmap for future space processors based on the RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) [7], and its heterogeneous architecture, combining FPGA fabric with RISC-V cores, is well suited to deterministic sensor acquisition and ML inference at the edge. The assembled prototype is shown in Figure 1.

The vibration sensing chain consists of two Kistler 8763B050BT05 tri-axial Integrated Electronics Piezo- Electric (IEPE) accelerometers, digitized by 24-bit Sigma- Delta Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) at 32 kSps per channel and interfaced to the FPGA via SPI. Phase currents of the flywheel and gimbal motors are measured using Hall-effect transducers and sampled at 3.3 kSps via I<sup>2</sup>C. Communication with the other modules follows the CAN bus standard (ISO 11898), while an additional Ethernet interface supports bulk data transfer for offline analysis.

blocks.title: CMG Equivalent System and Test Campaign

blocks.html: The device under test is the Quick MC2X2 DC marine gyroscopic stabilizer, a single-gimbal CMG with a rated flywheel speed of 6000 RPM and 551 Nms of angular momentum. In its original configuration, the gimbal precession is controlled passively. To replicate the active torque generation of satellite CMGs, the passive damper has been replaced with a servo drive coupled through a belt transmission, providing closed-loop angular positioning and velocity. The complete testbed assembly is shown in Figure 2.

blocks.html: The two tri-axial accelerometers are installed on the flywheel housing and gimbal frame, respectively, using rigid cyanoacrylate adhesive, selected to maximize mechanical coupling stiffness and preserve signal content throughout the diagnostic bandwidth [8]. Current transducers are mounted on the phase U of both the gimbal and flywheel motors.
The complete summary of the acquisition channels is provided in Table 1.

A controlled defect was introduced on the outer race of the flywheel bearing using Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM), producing a trench of width 0.25 mm and depth 2 mm, oriented perpendicular to the rolling direction, as shown in Figure 3. EDM is widely used in the literature on bearing diagnostics for its geometric precision and repeatability, allowing correlation between the known defect geometry and the resulting vibration signatures [9]. The damaged bearing was installed without modifying the original mounting interfaces, preserving the mechanical boundary conditions of the nominal configuration.

blocks.html: The damaged bearing introduced an additional resistive torque to the flywheel, resulting in the inability to reach the nominal 6000 RPM. This confirms the severity of the injected fault and defines the maximum speed limit of the degraded dataset.

The dataset was generated using two operational profiles that together cover the full speed envelope of the CMG. The first profile sweeps the flywheel from 1000 to 5000 RPM in discrete increments, acquiring data under both gimbalstatic conditions and during active gimbal maneuvers at each plateau. Above 5000 RPM, the acceleration of the flywheel becomes strongly nonlinear and stabilization requires longer ramp-up times; therefore, a dedicated second pattern was designed to cover the 6000 RPM operating point, following the same acquisition logic as the first. Thus, nominal acquisitions span the entire 1000 to 6000 RPM; degraded acquisitions are limited to 1000 to 5000 RPM, due to the torque saturation described in Section 3.2. The resulting dataset comprises several hundred valid acquisition files, ranging from a few seconds to several minutes in duration, covering both stationary and transient operating conditions across the full speed envelope.

As discussed in the previous sections, the reference architecture was selected to satisfy the constraints imposed by the target application, leading to the adoption of an autoencoder-based approach [10, 11]. This solution provides a suitable compromise between model complexity, computational cost, and detection performance. Autoencoders learn a compact representation of the input during the encoding stage and reconstruct the original signal during the decoding stage [12].

In this work, the autoencoder is trained exclusively on data collected under nominal operating conditions. The objective is therefore not to learn an explicit model of the faulty class, but rather to characterize the normal vibration behaviour of the system. During inference, samples consistent with the nominal operating regime are expected to be reconstructed accurately, whereas samples deviating from nominal behaviour are expected to produce larger reconstruction errors.

Each acquisition is segmented into non-overlapping windows of 1 s. For each window, the six vibration channels are transformed into time-frequency representations through the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), producing six 512 × 64 spectrograms. These spectrograms are stacked and used as a single model input tensor X ∈RC×H×W , with C = 6, H = 512, and W = 64. Consequently, anomaly detection is performed at window level: each 1 s segment is reconstructed by the autoencoder and assigned an MSE-based anomaly score.

blocks.html: A high value of s(X) indicates that the input window is poorly reconstructed by the autoencoder and is therefore less consistent with the nominal patterns learned during training. In a practical deployment, a decision threshold τ can be applied to the anomaly score. A window is classified as anomalous when

and as nominal otherwise. In this paper, however, no fixed operating threshold is imposed a priori. Instead, the MSE is evaluated as a continuous anomaly score. Detection performance is assessed by sweeping the threshold over the observed MSE range and computing the corresponding Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under the Curve (AUC). This allows the models to be compared independently of a single application-specific operating point. The AUC values reported in the results quantify the separability between nominal and anomalous windows across all possible MSE thresholds. The reconstructionerror distributions are also reported as a complementary qualitative tool to visualize the same separation in terms of anomaly score.

The nominal acquisitions are split into training, validation, and test subsets using a 70/15/15 ratio. No anomalous data is used during training, preserving the one-class nature of the approach. Anomalous acquisitions are used only during evaluation, together with unseen nominal samples, to assess the separability of the reconstruction-error scores.

Two model variants were developed to meet the constraints of the target hardware. The Convolutional AutoEncoder (CAE) follows a conventional design with a fully connected bottleneck at the encoder output, providing a compact explicit latent representation and resulting in 737K parameters. The Fully Convolutional AutoEncoder (FCAE) removes this dense layer, relying solely on convolutional downsampling to reduce dimensionality and reducing the model size to 230K parameters. Both architectures implement the same MSE-based anomaly detection procedure; they differ only in the encoder-decoder parameterization and in the resulting computational footprint.

The performance of the two autoencoders (CAE and FCAE) was evaluated on both nominal and anomalous datasets. For each model, 2000 windows were randomly sampled from each dataset, ensuring that all evaluation samples were unseen during training. The reconstruction error for each window was used as the anomaly score.

The reconstruction error distributions for nominal and anomalous windows are shown in Figure 4. For both models, a clear separation between the two classes is visible, with anomalous samples consistently producing higher reconstruction errors. The CAE exhibits a wider margin between distributions compared to the FCAE. Under this binary setting, both models achieve an AUC equal to 1.

Since the artificially induced defect produces strongly pronounced deviations from nominal behaviour, additional experiments were performed to evaluate model sensitivity to weaker anomalies by introducing intermediate severity levels. These were generated using a Variational Autoencoder [13] trained on both nominal and anomalous spectrograms. By traversing the learned latent space between the two operating conditions, synthetic samples with controlled degrees of degradation were produced, enabling a continuous evaluation of detection sensitivity.

Figure 5 reports the AUC as a function of anomaly severity. As severity decreases, the two architectures exhibit different behaviours. The CAE maintains higher AUC values at low severity levels, indicating greater robustness to weak anomalies. In contrast, the FCAE shows a more pronounced performance degradation.

To improve robustness against isolated false positives, a confirmation strategy is applied: the anomaly score of each window is replaced by the moving average over N consecutive windows. The right panel of Figure 5 shows the results for N = 8. This strategy significantly improves detection performance for both models, particularly benefiting the FCAE, which recovers AUC values comparable to those of the CAE at higher severity levels.

Finally, a reduced variant of the FCAE architecture, further optimized for the target hardware, was successfully deployed on the PolarFire SoC FPGA. Preliminary tests report an inference latency of 70 ms, confirming the feasibility of real-time onboard execution. A comprehensive analysis of the deployed model, including hardware–software codesign, quantization strategies, and resource utilization, is deferred to future work.

This paper presented MANUSAT, an edge-computing architecture for onboard CMG bearing fault detection integrating high-frequency vibration sensing with FPGA-based ML inference. Both autoencoder variants achieved perfect separation on severe faults; at reduced severity, the CAE proved more robust, while the FCAE recovered comparable performance through a moving-average confirmation strategy. Deployment on the PolarFire SoC confirmed real-time feasibility with 70 ms inference latency. Future work will address hardware–software co-design optimization, quantization effects, and the integration of additional telemetry signals (e.g., motor currents and thermal data) into the detection model, alongside in-orbit fine-tuning towards flight qualification.
